catalog_quote: SUPRASEGMENTAL ITEMS. It has been noted that Pawaian has fewer segmental phonemes than Kuman. This deficiency is compensated by the use of two suprasegmental phonemes, nasalization and tone. All six vowels may be oral or nasal and also carry either high or low tone. This means that potentially the six vowels can be used to form twenty-four different contrasts. In practice no more than three-way minimal pairs have been found. One often finds a difference in tone and a difference in nasalization, but nasalization never occurs on two of the words to form a four-way contrast. For example: [sú] tooth, [sù] ginger, [sų̀] road; [yɛ́] new, [yɛ̀] ancestor, [yɛ̨̀] type of nut.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pawaia is described as a tone language: every vowel (syllable) bears either high or low tone, and tone plus nasalization are the only suprasegmental phonemes named. No source opened says where word stress falls; none mentions stress for Pawaia at all, even the 2011 SIL Organised Phonology Data under a heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', which says only 'Tone is phonemic'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Trefry notes only that at most three-way (not four-way) tone/nasal minimal sets are attested and that tone is left unmarked in the practical orthography unless ambiguous.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical tone on vowels; examples are monosyllabic citation forms). Trefry's Pawaian data come from the Walio clan of the Karimui Plateau (18 months' fieldwork); the OPD is labelled Oyobe dialect. No phrase-level prosody is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language (ISO pwa, Glottolog pawa1255, also Pawaian/Pavaia/Aurama/Tudahwe/Sira/Yasa). Trefry 1969 is based on the Walio clan, Karimui Plateau (Eastern Highlands side); the SIL OPD is labelled 'Pawaia (Oyobe dialect)', Karimui, Chimbu & Gulf — Oyobe is the dialect Glottolog lists under pawa1255 (no separate glottocode).

sources.note: Phonological comparison pp. 7-15; 'Suprasegmental items' p. 13: Pawaian has two suprasegmental phonemes, nasalization and tone; every vowel oral/nasal and high or low tone; three-way minimal sets (su 'tooth', su 'ginger', su 'road' with tone/nasal differences). Note 3 p. 94: tone marks omitted in practical orthography unless ambiguous. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the book (full text checked with scanned spaces stripped).

sources.note: Section 3.51 'Phonological features: Pawaia' pp. 130-131, summarising Trefry 1969: 'A high-low tone system exists, and either tone may occur on all vowels'; syllables V, CV, VC, CVC; no consonant clusters. Nothing on stress for Pawaia (the word 'stress' on p. 131 concerns Witu; p. 117 concerns the pronunciation of the name Kewah). Summary p. 133: tone common to Daribi, Polopa, Pawaia and Witu.
